items.title: 12-year-old UCC student says he settled for Environmental Science after missing Medicine admission
items.description: Twelve-year-old Diamond Lucas, who has attracted national attention for gaining admission to the University of Cape Coast (UCC) at an unusually young age, has disclosed that his ambition was to study Medicine, but he was offered Environmental Science instead. Lucas said he had hoped to pursue a medical degree but did not meet the admission requirements for the programme after obtaining an aggregate 14 in the West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE). He was subsequently offered admission to study for a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science at UCC. The young student made this known during a meeting with the University’s Vice-Chancellor, Prof. Denis Worlanyo Aheto, who received him at his office. Despite the change in his preferred programme, Lucas said the meeting had boosted his morale and strengthened his resolve to work hard to meet the Vice-Chancellor’s expectations. UCC VC Prof. Denis Worlanyo Aheto and 12-year-old undergraduate Diamond Lucas. He expressed appreciation for the Vice-Chancellor’s interest in his welfare and the support he had received from the Department of Environmental Science. Prof. Aheto, in turn, encouraged the 12-year-old to remain focused on his academic journey and not allow negative comments about him on social media to distract him. “We are proud of you. Don’t mind what people are saying on social media,” he told Lucas. Read Also: Ignore the noise and stay focused – UCC VC to 12-year-old undergrad, Diamond Lucas He also urged the young undergraduate to use his time wisely, remain committed to excellence and uphold strong personal values, stressing that consistency, commitment and character were essential to success. Lucas has attracted considerable public interest following his admission to UCC at an age when many children are still in basic school. His academic journey had earlier drawn attention when he gained admission to Mfantsipim School at the age of nine. He was accompanied to the meeting by the Dean of the School of Biological Sciences, Prof. Ernest Kofi Amankwa Afrifa, and the Head of the Department of Environmental Science, Prof. Michael Miyittah-Kporgbe.

items.title: Présidentielle en France : le président du Sénat appelle à avancer la date du scrutin
items.description: Avec « une campagne qui doit s'arreter le vendredi, on imagine que le lendemain il n'y aurait pas d'expression ? » s'est interroge, le 18 novembre sur BFMTV, le president Les Republicains (LR) du Senat, Gerard Larcher, concernant le second tour de la presidentielle, fixe au lendemain du 1er mai. Rendez-vous a l'occasion duquel « s'expriment les syndicalistes et les politiques », a-t-il precise, avant d'assurer avoir « demande tres clairement qu'on avance la date de ces elections et je ne suis pas le seul a l'avoir demande ». « Qu'on ne me fasse pas croire que dans les corteges, dans les prises de position, il n'y aura aucun echo politique », s'etait deja offusque le 1er juillet sur le plateau d'Europe 1/CNews, dans la foulee de l'annonce de ces dates par le gouvernement, le president et candidat LR Bruno Retailleau. Celui-ci avait denonce un « choix qui n'est pas neutre », soulignant que les partis politiques avaient ete consultes sur differentes dates possibles, a savoir l'option choisie ou les 11 et 25 avril. « Le choix du gouvernement, ca a ete le choix de la gauche , parce que la gauche pense qu'un second tour apres le 1er mai, ca l'avantagera », avait encore fustige le senateur de Vendee et ex-ministre de l'Interieur. Présidentielle: "J'ai demandé qu'on avance la date de ces élections", déclare Gérard Larcher, président LR du Sénat https://t.co/HPreQ25ajl — BFM (@BFMTV) November 19, 2026 « C'est une manœuvre du president », avait aussi denonce le depute Rassemblement national (RN) du Nord et vice-president de l'Assemblee nationale, Sebastien Chenu, lors d'une conference de presse au Palais-Bourbon. « Juste apres les defiles du 1er mai, qui ont quelques connotations politiques, ce n'est pas particulierement judicieux si on veut respecter le silence electoral », avait-il souligne. « Je pense que ce serait intelligent » de changer ces dates, avait aussi juge Raphael Glucksmann, le 2 novembre, sur RMC/BFMTV. « Vu l'etat de polarisation, vu l'etat de detestation, vu l'etat de violence dans la societe, je pense que serait intelligent, effectivement, de changer la date de l'election », avait ajoute le candidat de la gauche non melenchoniste. « On sait gerer un 1er mai en France », avait assure – lors de l'annonce des dates – la porte-parole du gouvernement, Maud Bregeon, a peine quatre mois avant les pillages et des violences du 17 octobre. Certains observateurs de la vie politique francaise redoutent qu'a l'occasion des rassemblements du 1er mai, en cas de debordements, des bureaux de vote puissent etre attaques – notamment si Marine Le Pen etait presente au second tour – et ainsi empecher la bonne tenue du scrutin le lendemain. Pourrait egalement etre au second tour, a en croire les sondages, Jean-Luc Melenchon, le leader de la France insoumise, dont le parti avait ete pointe du doigt apres les violences autour du mouvement de grogne lyceen. « Nous n'accepterons jamais dans notre pays que le fascisme prenne le pouvoir legalement par les urnes, ce que veut faire Marine Le Pen », avait lance en fevrier la chef de file des deputes LFI, Mathilde Panot, se revendiquant de l'antifascisme. Fin octobre, Maud Bregeon avait exclu tout changement et refuse de « poser un genou a terre face aux delinquants, aux factieux » et aux « casseurs ». Constitutionnellement, le gouvernement francais a jusqu'a fin janvier pour modifier les dates de la presidentielle, le « decret de convocation » des electeurs devant etre publie au plus tard dix semaines avant la date du scrutin.

items.title: Attijariwafa bank : le résultat net gagne 11,7 % en neuf mois
items.description: Au 30 septembre 2026, le groupe affiche un résultat net de 10,7 milliards de dirhams, contre 9,6 milliards un an plus tôt. Alors que le produit net bancaire progresse de 3,7 %, la forte baisse du coût du risque (-38,2 %) porte notamment le résultat d’exploitation, en hausse de 10,1 %. Attijariwafa bank termine les neuf premiers mois de 2026 sur un résultat net de 10,7 milliards de dirhams, contre 9,6 milliards à fin septembre 2025, soit une hausse de 11,7 %. Le Conseil d’Administration, réuni le mardi 17 novembre 2026 sous la présidence de Mohamed El Kettani, a examiné l’activité et arrêté les comptes au 30 septembre 2026. Le résultat net part du groupe ressort pour sa part à 9,1 milliards de dirhams, contre 8,3 milliards à la même période de l’année précédente, en croissance de 10,3 %. Les tableaux de comptes précisent que la part des intérêts minoritaires s’établit à 1,5 milliard de dirhams, contre 1,3 milliard au 30 septembre 2025. Le produit net bancaire s’élève à 27,3 milliards de dirhams, en croissance de 3,7 % (+3,0 % à cours de change constants) par rapport à la même période de 2025. Cette progression est attribuée à une dynamique commerciale favorable, en termes de collecte de l’épargne et de financement de l’économie dans l’ensemble des pays de présence. Les dépôts et les crédits consolidés ont augmenté respectivement de 12,0 % et de 12,6 %, une variation mesurée entre le 30 septembre 2025 et le 30 septembre 2026. Le coût du risque recule de 38,2 % pour s’établir à 1,6 milliard de dirhams, contre 2,7 milliards un an plus tôt d’après les tableaux annexés au communiqué. Rapporté aux encours bruts de clientèle, il représente 0,43 % au titre des neuf premiers mois de 2026, contre 0,78 % à la même période en 2025. Cette forte baisse porte notamment le résultat d’exploitation, qui augmente de 10,1 % pour atteindre 15,6 milliards de dirhams. Le compte de résultat consolidé détaille les composantes de cette progression. La marge d’intérêt s’élève à 17,0 milliards de dirhams, contre 15,7 milliards au 30 septembre 2025, et la marge sur commissions à 5,4 milliards, contre 5,3 milliards. Le résultat brut d’exploitation atteint 17,2 milliards de dirhams, contre 16,8 milliards. La quote-part du résultat net des entreprises associées et des coentreprises mises en équivalence ressort à 0,8 milliard de dirhams, contre 0,4 milliard un an auparavant, et le résultat avant impôts à 16,4 milliards, contre 14,6 milliards. Côté bilan, la banque met en avant le renforcement de sa solidité financière. Les fonds propres consolidés s’établissent à 85,3 milliards de dirhams à fin septembre 2026, contre 77,8 milliards à fin septembre 2025, soit une augmentation de 9,7 %. La rentabilité des actifs (RoaA), calculée comme le rapport entre le résultat net et le bilan moyen, s’établit à 1,74 % à fin septembre 2026. La rentabilité sur les fonds propres (RoaE), rapportée à la moyenne des fonds propres, atteint 17,2 %. Le total du bilan consolidé ressort à 845,0 milliards de dirhams au 30 septembre 2026, contre 795,5 milliards au 31 décembre 2025. Pour ce qui est de l’activité de la banque au Maroc, le produit net bancaire s’élève à 16,2 milliards de dirhams au titre des neuf premiers mois de 2026, contre 15,7 milliards pour la même période de l’année dernière, soit une augmentation de 3,6 %. Les crédits à la clientèle enregistrent une hausse de 13,9 % à 318,9 milliards de dirhams et les dépôts une hausse de 12,0 % à 392,0 milliards, des variations mesurées entre le 30 septembre 2025 et le 30 septembre 2026. Ces évolutions renforcent le positionnement de la banque en tant que premier financeur de l’économie et premier collecteur de l’épargne. Dans les comptes sociaux, le résultat net de la période ressort à 6,9 milliards de dirhams, contre 6,7 milliards au 30 septembre 2025. The post Attijariwafa bank : le résultat net gagne 11,7 % en neuf mois appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: World: Food Price Monitoring and Analysis (FPMA) Bulletin #9, 12 November 2026
items.description: Country: World Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations Please refer to the attached file. Synopsis (short abstract) Global wheat and maize export prices declined in October 2026. Wheat prices fell amid subdued import demand and improving global production prospects, while maize prices declined from their September three‑year high amid seasonal harvest pressure in the United States of America and expectations of ample supplies from South America. Expectations of easing constraints on Black Sea export flows also weighed on wheat prices, although continued logistical disruptions in the region partly offset the downward pressure. By contrast, international rice prices increased, supported by harvest delays in some exporting countries, adverse weather conditions and rising production costs. In most domestic markets monitored by FAO, staple food prices remained relatively elevated in September and October 2026. In parts of East Africa and the Near East, conflict‑related market disruptions, currency depreciation and tight supplies continued to exert upward pressure on prices. In Far East Asia, weather-related production shortfalls and high production costs contributed to the increases in staple food prices, while in Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia, high transport and import costs continued to exert upward pressure on domestic food prices. By contrast, the arrival of new harvests improved market supplies and contributed to seasonal price declines in parts of West Africa and Central and South America. However, strong demand, delayed harvests and unfavourable production prospects continued to drive price increases in some markets. In Southern Africa, ample domestic supplies and continued intra-regional trade helped contain seasonal price increases.

items.title: Les enfants écrivent la Guinée de demain : quand la jeunesse guinéenne prend la plume pour façonner son avenir
items.description: À l'occasion de la célébration de la Journée internationale des droits de l'enfant, la Guinée a mis à l'honneur la parole et l'imagination de sa jeunesse autour d'un ouvrage collectif intitulé « Les enfants écrivent la Guinée de demain », fruit d'un concours national et d'une démarche participative portée notamment par l'UNICEF, les éditions L'Harmattan Guinée et les autorités nationales. L'événement a été marqué par une forte mobilisation institutionnelle, avec la présence remarquée du ministre Secrétaire général à la Présidence de la République, le Général Amara Camara, du ministre Directeur de Cabinet de la Présidence de la République, Djiba Diakité, ainsi que de nombreux membres du gouvernement et conseillers à la Présidence. Lancé environ un mois avant sa conclusion lors de cette célébration, le programme « Les enfants écrivent la Guinée de demain » a mobilisé des jeunes venus de différentes régions du pays, de Conakry à Kobikoro. Le concours national a enregistré mille cinq cents candidatures, témoignant d'un fort élan d'expression chez les enfants et les adolescents. Parmi l'ensemble des propositions reçues, trente textes ont été retenus pour figurer dans l'ouvrage. À travers ces pages, les jeunes auteurs partagent leurs rêves, leurs préoccupations et leurs attentes pour le pays, en recourant aussi bien aux mots qu'aux dessins et aux couleurs. Plusieurs visions se dessinent au fil des contributions : l'espoir d'une Guinée où chaque village dispose d'une école, le souhait d'une ville plus propre et plus verte, ou encore l'aspiration à un pays où aucun enfant n'est laissé de côté et où les droits de chacun sont respectés. Au-delà de la dimension littéraire et artistique, l'ouvrage entend rappeler que les enfants ne sont pas uniquement les citoyens de demain ou de simples bénéficiaires de politiques publiques : ils sont également des acteurs du présent dont la voix mérite d'être écoutée et prise en compte dans les réflexions qui touchent à leur avenir. Selon le Directeur général des Éditions L'Harmattan Guinée, Sansy Kaba Diakité, cette initiative s'inscrit dans une dynamique plus large de valorisation du capital humain et de participation enfantine, accompagnée par d'autres actions concrètes évoquées lors de la journée, telles que les ateliers Simandou expliqués aux enfants ou l'inauguration d'un point de lecture au jardin du 2 octobre afin d'encourager la lecture et l'écriture auprès du plus grand nombre. Moment fort de la cérémonie, la remise solennelle des prix a permis de saluer le talent et l'engagement des jeunes plumes distinguées par cette compétition : Troisième prix : remis à Sifa Naël ; Deuxième prix : attribué à Fatoumata Kadra Cissoko ; Prix coup de cœur : décerné à Tamila Sylla ; Prix coup de cœur illustration : revenu à Naofal Ninon Kah Koffi ; Prix du public : accordé à Hadja Salioudian Diallo ; Premier prix : remis à Fatoumata Birouane Diallo. Chacune de ces distinctions a été saluée par les applaudissements de l'assistance, réunissant autorités, partenaires, encadreurs et jeunes participants, avant de se conclure par l'inauguration d'un point de lecture dans l'enceinte du Jardin 2 octobre.

items.title: Mali : les défis du nouveau directeur général de l’INPS
items.description: L'Institut national de prevoyance sociale (INPS) a un nouveau directeur general. Nomme le 13 novembre dernier, il prend les commandes d'une structure confrontee a des accusations de mauvaise gestion, de detournement de fonds et de recrutements opaques. Entre lenteurs administratives, irregularites financieres et mecontentement des usagers, plusieurs defis l'attendent. Le nouveau responsable devra notamment assainir la gestion de l'Institut et restaurer la confiance des travailleurs et des retraites. Recouvrer les cotisations sociales et assurer le paiement des prestations aux travailleurs et aux retraites. Telles sont les principales missions de l'Institut national de prevoyance sociale. Mais depuis quelque temps, des difficultes dans le fonctionnement de la structure suscitent des inquietudes chez certains usagers et partenaires. Un gestionnaire des ressources humaines d'une entreprise privee, qui a souhaite garder l'anonymat, denonce notamment des lenteurs administratives dans le traitement des dossiers. Il evoque des difficultes liees au versement des allocations et a la prise en charge des accidents de travail. « Pour certains collaborateurs victimes d'accidents de travail, obtenir des indemnites c'est tout un probleme . » Certains finissent meme par y renoncer, deplore-t-il. La gestion financiere de l'institut « en cause » Au-dela des difficultes administratives, la gestion financiere et les pratiques de recrutement constituent egalement des preoccupations majeures. Dans son dernier rapport, le Bureau du Verificateur general (BVG) a releve plus de 15 milliards de francs CFA d'irregularites financieres dans la gestion de l'INPS entre 2021 et 2025. L'article sur ces irregularites a lire ici : INPS : le Verificateur General releve plus de 15 milliards de FCFA d'irregularites Assainir la gestion et renforcer les mecanismes de controle Pour Baba Boubacar Keïta, secretaire general de la Communaute de pratique en matiere de lutte contre la corruption, l'assainissement de l'Institut passe notamment par un renforcement des mecanismes de controle et la promotion de l'integrite au sein du personnel. Il denonce des pratiques de recrutement qui meritent, selon lui, davantage de transparence. « Les recrutements sont parfois suivis de licenciements ou de situations ou les personnes recrutees ne sont finalement pas retenues », constate-t-il. Il preconise ainsi la mise en place d'un systeme de controle efficace, accompagne de formations du personnel sur les questions d'integrite. Il recommande egalement la creation d'un mecanisme interne permettant aux travailleurs de signaler les pratiques irregulieres. Le nouveau directeur general est donc attendu sur plusieurs fronts. Ameliorer la qualite des services, renforcer la transparence dans la gestion, accelerer le traitement des dossiers et garantir une meilleure prise en charge des beneficiaires. Pourra-t-il redorer l'image de l'INPS aupres des Maliens notamment des travailleurs ? Les mois et les annees a venir nous le diront. L’article Mali : les défis du nouveau directeur général de l’INPS est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Government must account for each life lost to the galamsey fight – Effiduase Asokore MP
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Effiduase Asokore, Dr. Nana Ayew Afriyie, says the Minority is committed to holding the government to account for each life lost in the fight against illegal mining (galamsey). This follows a clash between personnel of the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS) and residents of Manso Keniago, which left six people dead and many injured. According to him, government must investigate the deaths and hold those found culpable to account. “And definitely we are going to make sure each blood among these is accounted for. We will do that. We will ensure that. We will make sure that each of these people and their families are given justice, and justice duly served them,” he said. The lawmaker made the statement on the floor of parliament during a debate on the 2027 budget statement. He believes the government’s fight against illegal mining has failed. The shooting incident happened on 11 November 2026 during an operation against illegal mining in the Amansie South District of the Ashanti Region. Residents and traditional authorities say the confrontation began after a dispute over the removal of excavators seized by the NAIMOS task force. They objected to the equipment being transported through the community along a newly tarred road, and asked that it be moved on a low-bed truck instead. The Chief, Nana Obeng Mensah Ababio II, has alleged that residents were subjected to gunfire without provocation. But NAIMOS has refuted the allegations, claiming the community opened fire on its personnel. The lawmaker wants the government to fully investigate the matter.

items.title: Ignore the noise and stay focused – UCC VC to 12-year-old undergrad, Diamond Lucas
items.description: The Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cape Coast (UCC), Prof. Denis Worlanyo Aheto, has urged 12-year-old undergraduate Diamond Lucas to remain focused on his academic journey and ignore negative comments about him on social media. Prof. Aheto gave the advice when he received the young student, who has attracted national attention for gaining admission to UCC at an unusually young age to study for a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science. The Vice-Chancellor encouraged Lucas to make good use of his time, stressing that students who managed their time effectively were better positioned to identify opportunities and excel in their endeavours. He described excellence as the relentless pursuit of quality, which requires consistency and commitment, and urged the young undergraduate to uphold strong values, noting that character shapes destiny. “We are proud of you. Don’t mind what people are saying on social media,” Prof. Aheto told him. Lucas, who previously made headlines after gaining admission to Mfantsipim School at the age of nine, thanked the Vice-Chancellor for taking an interest in his welfare and acknowledged the support he had received from UCC’s Department of Environmental Science. He said the meeting had boosted his morale and motivated him to work harder to meet the Vice-Chancellor’s expectations. The 12-year-old disclosed that his initial ambition was to study Medicine. However, after obtaining an aggregate 14 in the West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE), he did not meet the admission requirements for the programme and was subsequently offered a place in Environmental Science. His admission to UCC marks another milestone in an academic journey that has drawn considerable public interest, following his progression to senior high school at an age when many children are still in basic school. He was accompanied to the meeting by the Dean of the School of Biological Sciences, Prof. Ernest Kofi Amankwa Afrifa, and the Head of the Department of Environmental Science, Prof. Michael Miyittah-Kporgbe.

items.title: 'We don't want to die': Protesters slam Claude creator Anthropic after IPO debut
items.description: Around a hundred people braved the rain on Thursday to protest in front of Anthropic’s offices in San Francisco, the same day the artificial intelligence (AI) lab went public , to denounce its race toward ever more powerful AI models. “Ban RSI, we don’t want to die,” the protesters chanted. They were referring to recursive self-improvement (RSI) — a term the industry uses to describe building advanced AI models that can autonomously create newer versions of themselves, which critics worry will hasten doomsday scenarios. “Don’t invest in extinction,” one sign said. “These people are going to make a profit off of a technology that even they admit has a chance of eliminating life on Earth, or human life on Earth,” Tarnel Abbott, a 72-year-old retired librarian, said at Thursday’s protest. Another protester, Emily Tan, who travelled from Los Angeles, described the situation as “a black box.” “Most people in the country, even in SF, do not know what is happening,” Tan, 31, said. The protesters’ first demand: ban RSI. “There are only a few places in the world where recursive self-improvement is possible in 2027, and this office is one of them,” Jacob Coxon said. Coxon is a young researcher whose resignation from Anthropic, and accompanying warnings about AI safety, caused a major stir back in September. People in Silicon Valley admit in private that they don’t want RSI to be developed anytime soon, Coxon said. Anthropic, which on Thursday pulled off the largest IPO in history, says it has not yet reached the RSI stage. The ‘good guys’ Critics question whether a company like Anthropic, which talks about prioritising safety over profits, can stick to its stated values while facing pressure from shareholders, who want to see growth and a return on their investment. “They are talking about trying to slow this down and doing pacing, but (…) they’re not, like, trying that hard,” said Tyler Tracy, 26, a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit called Redwood Research. Anthropic was founded by several former OpenAI employees who disagreed with its business decisions and vowed to always prioritise safety. “Stop the AI race,” another protest sign said. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI employee, said friends at both labs answer his fears by arguing that if they don’t build it, a rival or China will, and that they are “the responsible good guys”. “I don’t like that answer, and that’s why I’m here protesting,” Kokotajlo said. He now heads a research organisation called the AI Futures Project. Many of the protesters acknowledged they still use AI tools and consider them helpful, but they feel it is advancing too quickly and without sufficient safeguards. A day earlier, an open letter signed by researchers, entrepreneurs, and academics accused Anthropic of not being “a safe AI company.” A sole counter-protester, 31-year-old activist blogger Barak Gila, stood in front of the crowd holding a sign that thanked Anthropic for building the technology and generating a sizable local economic impact. A demonstrator confronted him, but Gila was all smiles, even delighted at the prospect of a clash. “Without Anthropic, I’m gonna die for sure, right? With Anthropic, maybe I’ll live 10 years longer,” Gila said. “Or maybe you’ll die in like two years,” the other demonstrator responded.

items.title: World: Crop Prospects and Food Situation Triannual Global Report No. 3, November 2026
items.description: Country: World Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations Please refer to the attached file. Synopsis (short abstract) The triannual Crop Prospects and Food Situation report provides a forward-looking global analysis of cereal production, market trends and acute food security conditions, with a particular attention on low-income food-deficit countries. FAO estimates that 41 countries/territories require external assistance for food: 31 in Africa, eight in Asia, one in Latin America and the Caribbean, and one in Europe. Persisting conflicts and insecurity remain the primary drivers of the most severe levels of acute food insecurity, while weather shocks associated with the strong El Niño event are worsening conditions in several subregions. Looking ahead, El Niño-related impacts on production are expected to remain severe into 2027 in several subregions, likely aggravating acute food insecurity further. The report also includes FAO's latest forecast for 2026 cereal production among the Low-Income Food-Deficit Countries (LIFDCs), pegged at 126.5 million tonnes, about 2 percent above both the 2025 level and the five-year average. The increase largely reflects a strong production recovery in Asia, particularly in Near East Asia, while production among African LIFDCs is expected to remain near-average.

items.title: Cagliari : Fabio Pisacane met en garde Paul Mendy après ses débuts remarqués chez les Lions

Son entraineur Fabio Pisacane a toutefois tenu à envoyer un message clair à son protégé. Paul Mendy a connu des débuts idylliques. Pour sa deuxième entrée en jeu le lundi 16 novembre 2026, l’attaquant de 19 ans a marqué son premier but avec le Sénégal. Des débuts tonitruants qui ont fait réagir son entraineur à Cagliari, Fabio Pisacane. Ce dernier, satisfait, a toutefois enjoint son poulain à travailler davantage. « À l’heure actuelle, je ne pense pas qu’il se laisse distraire par ce qui lui arrive. Il a brûlé les étapes (passé très vite des U19 au groupe pro NDLR), mais il sait que le football est une usine à illusions. Aujourd’hui, tu es un phénomène ; demain, tu risques de te blesser. Il sait qu’il doit continuer à travailler. Il est très concentré. Si vous me demandez s’il était plus heureux ces derniers jours, je dirais que oui, mais il est toujours souriant », a-t-il lancé en conférence de presse ce vendredi 20 novembre 2026. items.title: MultiChoice cuts entry-level DStv, GOtv subscriptions to ₦6,000
items.description: MultiChoice Nigeria has introduced restructured DStv and GOtv subscription packages, with entry-level options starting at ₦6,000, following customer feedback on affordability and content preferences. The company’s Chief Executive Officer, Kemi Omotosho, disclosed this during an interview on the Global Business Report on ARISE News on Friday, saying the new packages were designed to simplify subscription choices and provide customers with access to entertainment, sports and other content. She said the company had listened to its subscribers and adjusted its offerings to better address their needs. “We recognised that our customers are dear to us, so we listened to our customers, we simplified our offerings,” she said. Under the new arrangement, DStv subscribers can choose from four packages: Starter, Select, Sports and Premium, while GOtv offers Easy, Starter, Select and Sports. Omotosho said the Starter package, which costs ₦6,000, provides access to more than 90 channels, including Africa Magic Plus, the Premier League Match of the Week, selected UEFA Champions League matches and La Liga coverage. She also explained that the Sports package had been redesigned from the former Compact offering to provide broader access to major sporting competitions. According to her, the package includes all Premier League and Champions League matches, as well as UFC and WWE content, alongside channels available on the Starter and Select packages. Clarifying the subscription rates, Omotosho said the Sports package costs ₦21,000 for new subscribers, while the ₦19,000 rate applies only to existing Compact subscribers migrating to the new package. “When you move into the new pack, it’s ₦21,000 on the Sports pack,” she said. The CEO also highlighted the benefits of MultiChoice Nigeria’s integration into the Canal+ Group, which operates in more than 70 countries across Africa, Asia and Europe. She said the integration had strengthened the company’s capacity in content acquisition, technology and partnerships while retaining its focus on the Nigerian market. “We’re basically riding on global muscle, but we still want to be very relevant to the Nigerian consumer,” she stated. On the company’s transition towards digital entertainment, Omotosho said MultiChoice regarded satellite television and streaming services as complementary platforms rather than competing products. “For us, streaming is not an ‘either/or,’ it is ‘and’,” she said. She cited DStv Stream, which enables subscribers to access television content online without a satellite dish or decoder. According to her, the company’s technology-agnostic approach allows customers to choose satellite television for reliability in areas with limited broadband access or streaming services for greater flexibility. Reflecting on developments since Canal+ acquired MultiChoice, Omotosho highlighted the reduction in the price of new satellite bundles to ₦15,000, the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards (AMVCA), an exclusive FIFA World Cup campaign and increased collaboration with regulatory agencies to tackle piracy. She disclosed that the company was working with the National Broadcasting Commission, Nigerian Copyright Commission and Nigerian Communications Commission to address the challenge. Describing piracy as an economic problem, she warned that its persistence could undermine investment and funding for Nigeria’s creative industry. Omotosho said the company’s five-year strategy was focused on expanding its reach across the continent, with a target of making its services available in one out of every two African households by 2030. items.title: Bagbin urges Africa to take charge of its global narrative
items.description: Speaker of Parliament Alban Sumana Kingsford Bagbin has called on African countries to strengthen their communication systems and take greater ownership of how the continent is portrayed to the rest of the world. He said Africa’s image was often shaped by external narratives that failed to reflect its diversity, complexities and aspirations, making it necessary for Africans to communicate their own experiences and development priorities. Addressing delegates at the 2026 World Public Relations Forum in Abuja, Nigeria, Mr Bagbin stressed that the call for greater African control of the continent’s narrative should not be mistaken for propaganda or the selective presentation of information. Rather, he said, Africa needed an authentic voice built on evidence, professional integrity and confidence in its collective potential. “Africa’s story must be communicated by Africans,” he said, adding that the continent’s democratic progress would depend on ensuring that citizens were heard and had a meaningful role in decisions affecting their future. On the growing influence of technology, the Speaker urged stakeholders to place ethical considerations, human rights, data protection and freedom of expression at the centre of digital innovation. Citing Ghana’s Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843), he warned that technological advancement must not undermine citizens’ privacy, dignity and fundamental rights. He also advocated greater investment in media and information literacy to equip young people with the skills to identify misinformation and assess the credibility of information sources. He called for efforts to eliminate communication that promotes hatred and division. Mr Bagbin further highlighted Ghana’s efforts to promote transparency and public participation, insisting that democratic institutions should be responsive to the people. “Must not only speak to the people; they must also listen to the people,” he said, describing citizen engagement as essential to open governance. He cited initiatives such as Citizens in Focus, which enables Members of Parliament to sponsor statements on behalf of constituents, and Parliament Aayalolo, an outreach programme that gathers views from citizens and associations to inform legislation. He also pointed to the Right to Information Act, 2019 (Act 989), as an important step towards strengthening transparency. Mr Bagbin, who is also President of the Conference of Speakers and Presidents of African Legislatures (CoSPAL), used the occasion to invite legislative leaders to the organisation’s 4th General Assembly in Liberia from December 9 to 11, 2026. The forum, organised by the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations with support from the African Public Relations Association, also marks the 25th anniversary of the Global Alliance for Public Relations and Communication Management.

items.title: Retraites et pensions des veuves : les hausses annoncées dès janvier 2027
items.description: Présentant les mesures prévues dans le cadre du PLF 2027 devant la commission des finances de la Chambre des conseillers, le ministre de l’Économie, des Finances, et de la Performance publique, Fouzi Lekjaa, a détaillé le relèvement des pensions des veuves et la revalorisation progressive du minimum de retraite jusqu’à 3.000 dirhams à l’horizon 2030. Ces deux dispositifs devraient concerner plusieurs centaines de milliers de bénéficiaires. Les veuves bénéficiaires du régime de l’aide sociale directe et les retraités percevant de faibles pensions sont au cœur de deux mesures annoncées par le gouvernement. Lors de la discussion générale du projet de loi de finances 2027, vendredi devant la commission des finances et de la planification à la Chambre des conseillers, Fouzi Lekjaa a précisé les modalités et le coût de ces dispositifs, dont la mise en œuvre doit commencer en janvier prochain. À fin octobre 2026, le nombre de veuves bénéficiant de l’aide sociale directe s’élevait à 434.196, soit 11% de l’ensemble des ménages bénéficiaires. Parmi elles, 89.120 veuves ont des enfants à charge. Le ministre a annoncé le relèvement de leur taux de pension de 50% à 100%. Selon les chiffres présentés, plus de 431.334 veuves devraient bénéficier de cette mesure, pour un coût annuel estimé à 7,33 milliards de dirhams. La répartition concerne quatre régimes : 205.413 bénéficiaires relevant de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS), pour un coût de 2,27 milliards de dirhams, 117.353 relevant du régime des pensions civiles, pour 3,083 milliards, 63.905 du régime des pensions militaires, pour 835 millions, et 44.663 affiliées au Régime collectif d’allocation de retraite (RCAR), pour 1,143 milliard de dirhams. Le minimum de retraite porté progressivement à 3.000 dirhams Autre mesure détaillée par Fouzi Lekjaa : le relèvement progressif du minimum des pensions de retraite à 3.000 dirhams. Le dispositif vise les personnes percevant actuellement les minima théoriques, fixés à 1.500 dirhams dans le secteur public et à 1.000 dirhams auprès de la CNSS, mais aussi les retraités dont les pensions dépassent ces montants sans atteindre le nouveau seuil. La revalorisation sera échelonnée sur quatre étapes : le minimum de retraite passera à 1.700 dirhams à partir de janvier 2027, puis à 2.000 dirhams en janvier 2028, à 2.500 dirhams en 2029 et enfin à 3.000 dirhams au début de l’année 2030. Cette mesure devrait bénéficier à quelque 557.472 personnes dans un premier temps, dont 180.000 veuves, pour un coût prévisionnel de 3,3 milliards de dirhams. Le nombre de bénéficiaires devrait atteindre 1,2 million en 2031, selon les projections présentées par le ministre. © Mounir Mehimdate 8.000 postes budgétaires prévus dans la santé Au cours de la même intervention, Fouzi Lekjaa est également revenu sur les recrutements prévus dans le secteur de la santé en 2027. Au total, 8.000 postes sont annoncés, dans le cadre d'une approche visant à atteindre un ratio de 35 professionnels de santé pour 10.000 habitants. Ces postes se répartissent entre 5.400 postes budgétaires inscrits au budget du ministère de la Santé et 2.600 postes que les six groupements sanitaires territoriaux devront créer sur leurs budgets propres. Cette organisation s’inscrit dans le cadre de la réforme de la gouvernance du secteur et vise à adapter les recrutements aux besoins de chaque région. 106,9 MMDH pour l’éducation nationale Concernant l’éducation nationale, le ministre a indiqué que les crédits alloués au secteur atteindront 106,9 milliards de dirhams en 2027, soit une augmentation de 4,7 milliards par rapport à l’exercice précédent. À ces crédits s’ajoutent les contributions de la Fondation Mohammed VI de promotion des œuvres sociales de l’éducation-formation, estimées à près de 1,3 milliard de dirhams, ainsi que celles des régions au financement des projets éducatifs. © Mounir Mehimdate Fouzi Lekjaa a également insisté sur la nécessité d’améliorer la planification et l’efficacité de la dépense publique, notamment à travers une meilleure identification des besoins réels des établissements, en tenant compte des évolutions démographiques et des spécificités territoriales. L’objectif affiché est d’optimiser la répartition des ressources humaines et des investissements dans le secteur. items.title: Mahama commissions DNA laboratory to strengthen Ghana’s forensic investigations
items.description: President John Mahama has commissioned a national Human Identification Laboratory at the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research to strengthen Ghana’s capacity to conduct DNA testing for criminal investigations, disaster victim identification and disputed family relationships. The facility, popularly known as the DNA Laboratory, will provide local testing services for forensic investigations, paternity and maternity disputes, and inheritance-related cases, reducing the country’s reliance on foreign laboratories for specialised analysis. Commissioning the facility alongside new vaccine research and development laboratories, President Mahama said the investment would address a longstanding gap in Ghana’s forensic and emergency response systems. He recalled that following the August 2025 helicopter crash, which claimed eight lives, Ghana had to transport tissue samples recovered from the accident scene to South Africa for DNA analysis. The process left families waiting several days for the identification of their relatives, an experience he described as a moment of shame for the country. President Mahama said the new facility would enable Ghana to handle similar incidents more quickly and independently, while strengthening its ability to resolve complex criminal cases. Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh said the laboratory was established in response to a directive from the President following the helicopter disaster. He explained that although Ghana had qualified scientists capable of conducting DNA analysis, the country lacked the specialised equipment required to carry out the tests locally. On the vaccine research and development laboratories, Mr Akandoh said the facilities would strengthen efforts to build local capacity for vaccine production, with the first vaccines bottled in Ghana expected to be on the market in 2027. Chief Executive Officer of the National Vaccine Institute, Dr Sodzi Sodzi-Tettey, said Ghana was making progress towards establishing a sustainable vaccine manufacturing ecosystem. He disclosed that the first of three bulk substances required for the targeted vaccine production was already in the country at Atlantic LifeSciences. He added that the government was pursuing long-term procurement arrangements to guarantee a market for vaccines manufactured locally. The two projects form part of Ghana’s broader efforts to strengthen domestic scientific capacity, improve health security and reduce dependence on foreign expertise and supplies.

items.title: Ghana Air Force receives second of four new helicopters
items.description: The Ghana Air Force has taken delivery of an Airbus ACH160 helicopter, the second of four aircraft being acquired by the government to strengthen the military’s aviation capabilities. The helicopter arrived at the Air Force Base in Accra on Friday, November 20, 2026, following the delivery of an Airbus ACH175 in March this year. In a Facebook post announcing the arrival, the Air Force said the four helicopters were being procured for phased delivery to expand its existing fleet and improve its capacity to support national security operations. The acquisition is expected to boost operational readiness and strengthen the military’s ability to discharge its constitutional responsibilities while supporting the country’s broader development objectives. The ACH160 comes with advanced aviation technology, including the Helionix digital cockpit, which provides pilots with improved situational awareness and flight management capabilities. Its twin-engine configuration and modern rotor design are also intended to enhance efficiency, reduce noise and deliver smoother flight operations. The helicopter features a spacious cabin designed to improve passenger comfort, making it suitable for executive transportation and other assigned missions. The Ghana Air Force said the aircraft’s delivery journey started in Marignane, France, and took it through Spain and North-West Africa before proceeding along the West African Atlantic coast to Ghana. The arrival brings to two the number of helicopters delivered under the government’s four-aircraft acquisition programme, with two more expected to follow in subsequent phases.

items.title: Lydia Forson backs Sarkodie’s call for investment in Ghana’s film industry
items.description: Ghanaian actress Lydia Forson has thrown her support behind Sarkodie’s recent call for greater investment in Ghana’s film industry. According to her, the creative sector’s economic and cultural value remains underestimated. Responding to the rapper’s concerns, Lydia said the conversation about the creative sector’s potential was long overdue, arguing that film, music and other creative works could help attract tourism, business and investment to the country. In a post on X, she said she had discussed the same issue with a group of executives from different fields, questioning why Ghana continued to underestimate the influence of film and the creative industry. “Film, music, advertising and the media can make you curious enough about a place to book a flight, do business there or consider investing in it,” she wrote. Citing Hollywood’s model, Lydia noted that many people developed an interest in visiting the United States through films long before they could afford to travel there. She believes Ghana has a similar opportunity if it takes seriously the people who tell its stories and the resources required to promote those stories to international audiences. Forson also challenged public perceptions of the financial rewards of acting and other creative professions, recounting an encounter with someone who expressed surprise at how much actors could earn. She said the reaction had stayed with her because it reflected a wider tendency to appreciate the entertainment creatives provide without recognising the business and economic activities behind it. “A single day on a film set can put 30 people to work, some of whom are paid that very day,” she said, explaining that actors, musicians and other creatives spend money on services such as hair, make-up and clothing, while creating income opportunities for other professionals. She further argued that endorsement deals were not simply payments for an artiste’s popularity but represented access to an audience and the trust built with that audience over time. The celebrated actress said the creative industry’s contribution to everyday life was often overlooked, despite the extent to which people rely on music, films, news, advertising and other forms of creative work. “We rely on this work every day, and when it comes time to draw up a budget, we still talk about funding it as though we’re doing somebody a favour,” she wrote. Lydia Forson pushed back against calls for filmmakers to simply produce better films, arguing that quality production alone was not enough without adequate resources for marketing and distribution. She mentioned the attention generated by American internet personality IShowSpeed around a Ghanaian documentary as an example of the importance of promotion and audience reach. “His involvement put it in front of an audience it had struggled to reach. Making the work and getting people to see it are two different jobs. Both need a budget,” she said. Lydia, however, acknowledged that creatives also had responsibilities in building a sustainable industry. She urged practitioners to take their craft, professional agreements and delivery more seriously, while encouraging greater openness about the business side of their work. She said creatives needed to work together to improve their earning conditions, particularly when negotiating fees, noting that it was difficult to secure better pay when some practitioners accepted rates that barely covered the cost of their work. Reflecting on Ghana’s cultural history, Forson also referenced the importance former President Osagyefo Dr Kwame Nkrumah placed on culture in projecting the country internationally. She called for a similar commitment today, suggesting that it should be reflected in budgets for production and marketing, how institutions commission and pay creatives, and whose work Ghana showcases when promoting itself abroad. “We already have people doing extraordinary work here. Imagine what Ghana could do if we treated their work as seriously as we treat the ambitions we have for this country,” she added. Lydia Forson’s comments follow a post by rapper Sarkodie on Thursday, 19 November 2026, in which he urged the government to increase investment in Ghana’s film industry. Comparing Hollywood’s influence on global perceptions of the United States with Africa’s storytelling potential, Sarkodie argued that film could help attract tourism and investment while promoting Ghanaian and African identity. He also criticised the creative sector’s treatment in national budget allocations and called on the government to recognise film as a tool for nation-building and international promotion.

items.title: AI-generated fake content threatens democracy, national security – Okonkwo
items.description: By Dickson Omobola Executive Chairman of United Nigeria Airlines, Professor Obiora Okonkwo, has expressed concerns over the growing sophistication of artificial intelligence, AI, saying its capacity to generate convincing fake images, videos and voices poses fresh threats to democracy, national security and public trust, particularly during elections. Okonkwo warned that hate speech, misinformation and irresponsible communication could be as destructive as weapons, saying the 1994 Rwandan genocide was an example of how manipulated information could incite mass violence, destroy lives and destabilise nations. He spoke while delivering the opening address at the African session of the World Public Relations Forum, WPRF, Abuja 2026, where he challenged journalists, public relations practitioners, advertisers and corporate communication professionals to strengthen self-regulation and uphold ethical standards to prevent communication platforms from becoming instruments of propaganda and social division. Speaking on the theme, ‘Responsible Communication in Africa: The Importance of Self-Regulation and Information and Media Literacy,’ he said the influence of communication demanded greater responsibility from those who shaped public opinion. He said: “The lesson is unmistakable. Communication is not always an innocent exercise. In the hands of irresponsible actors, the microphone can become as disruptive as a very dangerous weapon.” He said the 2023 general elections were an example of the dangers of irresponsible communication, adding that although social media facilitated political mobilisation, it also enabled the circulation of fabricated election results, unverified claims and divisive ethnic and political narratives. He recalled that the European Union Election Observation Mission documented misleading political communication during the polls, warning that such practices could undermine public confidence in democratic institutions and citizens’ ability to make informed electoral choices. He said: “In an age of unprecedented information flow, the credibility, integrity and social value of what we communicate are as important as the freedom and the platforms through which we communicate.” The airline chairman also cited the COVID-19 pandemic, when the World Health Organisation identified an infodemic of false and misleading information that confused populations, encouraged risky behaviour and weakened confidence in public health institutions. He said misinformation surrounding Ebola outbreaks in parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo similarly fuelled distrust of health workers and undermined disease-control interventions. “These examples demonstrate that irresponsible communication can threaten not only democratic stability but also human lives,” he warned. Okonkwo maintained that the emergence of AI-generated content had made information verification more urgent, particularly as digital platforms increasingly allowed individuals to publish and distribute information without traditional editorial safeguards. He explained that information literacy enabled citizens to identify credible sources and evaluate evidence, while media literacy helped them understand how messages were produced, framed and distributed. He said: “In an age when almost anyone with a smartphone can become a publisher and distributor of information, the ability to question, verify and critically assess information is an essential requirement of citizenship.” The post AI-generated fake content threatens democracy, national security – Okonkwo appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Rivers 2027: Dumo appoints Wike’s ex-commissioner campaign strategist
items.description: By Daniel Abia, P/Harcourt Ahead of the 2027 governorship election in Rivers State, governorship candidate, Dumo Lulu-Briggs, has appointed a former Commissioner for Information and Communications under the administration of former Governor Nyesom Wike, Dr Austin Tam-George, as Director of Strategy and Public Policy of his campaign council. The appointment was announced in a statement issued on Friday in Port Harcourt by Sotonye Ijuye-Dagogo, Directorate of Media and Publicity, Dumo Lulu-Briggs Governorship Campaign Council. The campaign council said the appointment underscored its commitment to intellectual depth, strategic planning, policy innovation, implementation and effective public engagement as it pursued its vision for a more prosperous, inclusive and economically transformed Rivers State. It described Tam-George as bringing a combination of academic distinction, public-sector experience, international exposure and professional expertise in strategic communications, governance and public policy to the campaign. Tam-George holds a PhD from the University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa, and is an alumnus of the Senior Executive Fellows programme at Harvard University’s John F. Kennedy School of Government, where he studied leadership and public policy. He was also an Andrew W. Mellon Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the University of Cape Town, South Africa, and received executive education at IESE Business School, University of Navarra, Spain. The statement said he is a member of the Harvard Business Review Advisory Council, an invitation-only research community of business professionals. His professional experience spans academia, government, international development, corporate affairs and strategic advisory services. He has taught at institutions including the University of Cape Town and Pan-Atlantic University. The campaign council also highlighted his engagements with international institutions, including UNESCO and the New Partnership for Africa’s Development (NEPAD), particularly in governance, education, youth development and institutional capacity building. It recalled his tenure as Commissioner for Information and Communications in Rivers State, during which it said he demonstrated professional management of public communication and commitment to the state’s development. According to the statement, Tam-George will provide strategic leadership in coordinating the campaign’s strategy, public policy framework and communications architecture. Commenting on the appointment, Lulu-Briggs said he remained committed to assembling a team of accomplished professionals and experienced individuals capable of contributing to the restructuring of governance and development in Rivers State. “I am delighted to welcome Dr Austin Tam-George to our team as we continue to hold robust conversations on our agenda for Rivers State,” he said. items.title: United Nigeria Airlines begins Jos flights to Lagos, Kano, Owerri
items.description: United Nigeria Airlines will commence scheduled flight operations from Jos to Lagos, Kano and Owerri on November 24 and 29, 2026, providing residents of Plateau State with additional air connections to other parts of the country. The airline said tickets for the new routes were already available for purchase. The Lagos–Jos–Lagos route will operate four times weekly on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays, while the Jos–Kano–Jos and Jos–Owerri–Jos routes will each operate twice weekly. Flights between Jos and Kano will operate on Tuesdays and Fridays, while those between Jos and Owerri will run on Wednesdays and Sundays. However, because the Owerri airport is currently closed, operations on the Jos–Owerri route will commence on Sunday, November 29, five days after the initial launch date. The development follows the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Plateau State Government and United Nigeria Airlines on Monday, November 9, at the office of the Commissioner for Transport, Jatau Gyang, in Jos. Under the agreement, the airline will introduce scheduled services on the Jos–Kano and Jos–Owerri routes, which the state government said were previously not served. Speaking after the signing, Gyang said the partnership was part of the state government’s broader efforts to position Plateau as a leading destination for investment, tourism, commerce and economic opportunities. He commended the airline’s management for its confidence in the state’s vision. According to him, the Jos–Owerri route will ease movement between Plateau and the South-East and South-South regions, thereby supporting trade, investment, tourism and social exchanges. He said the Jos–Kano connection would further strengthen Plateau’s relationship with the North-West, which he described as home to major commercial and industrial centres offering opportunities for business partnerships and trade. Responding on behalf of the airline, its Managing Director, Mazi Osita Okonkwo, said the agreement was significant because it would connect the South-East, South-West and North-Central regions. He described Plateau as a strategic state and assured that the airline would maintain its service standards. Okonkwo also commended Governor Caleb Mutfwang for his vision and strategic direction, while acknowledging Gyang’s efforts in facilitating the agreement. Passengers can book flights through the airline’s website, mobile application or accredited travel agents. The post United Nigeria Airlines begins Jos flights to Lagos, Kano, Owerri appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Health Ministry pushes integration of traditional medicine into mainstream healthcare
items.description: The Ministry of Health has highlighted the role of traditional medicine in expanding access to healthcare, particularly in rural and underserved communities, as Ghana joined other stakeholders to mark the 24th African Traditional Medicine Day and the 27th Ghana Traditional Medicine Week. Deputy Minister of Health, Prof. Dr Grace Ayensu-Danquah, said integrating indigenous medicinal knowledge with scientific research was critical to improving the safety, quality and effectiveness of traditional treatments. She made the remarks while delivering the keynote address at the celebration, held under the theme, “ Reflection on Research and Development Efforts of Traditional Medicine Towards Achieving Universal Health Coverage in the African Region .” Prof. Ayensu-Danquah noted that traditional medicine remained an important source of healthcare for millions of people, particularly those with limited access to conventional health services. She cited the training of about 600 medical herbalists at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) and the establishment of herbal medicine units in 55 public hospitals as key steps towards integrating traditional medicine into Ghana’s mainstream healthcare system. The Deputy Minister said the Ministry was also prioritising the documentation and protection of indigenous medicinal knowledge, as well as expanding herbal medicine services to Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) compounds and sub-district health facilities. Other priorities include protecting intellectual property rights and supporting the local production of standardised herbal medicines. She urged researchers, traditional medicine practitioners, regulatory institutions and development partners to deepen collaboration to translate indigenous knowledge and scientific discoveries into safe and effective healthcare solutions. The celebration provided a platform for stakeholders to review progress in the sector, share experiences and explore ways to strengthen research, innovation and regulation. It also highlighted the importance of bridging indigenous knowledge and modern science to preserve Ghana’s medicinal heritage and make traditional medicine a safe and effective component of an inclusive and resilient healthcare system.

items.title: University of America challenges NUC over illegal operations
items.description: By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo The National Universities Commission (NUC) and the University of America, Curaçao, have disagreed over the legality of the institution’s academic operations in Nigeria, with the commission warning prospective students against seeking admission into its programmes. The NUC had declared the institution’s operations in Nigeria illegal, alleging that it was admitting students, running academic programmes and claiming to award degrees through unauthorised campuses and learning centres across the country. However, the university has challenged the commission’s position, insisting that its legal existence as a foreign institution is distinct from the regulatory status of its learning support centres in Nigeria. In a public notice issued on Tuesday, the NUC’s Director of Public Affairs, Rita Okonjo, said the institution, also known as the University of America, had not been authorised to operate or award degrees in Nigeria. She identified the centres allegedly linked to the institution as Cosmopolitan International Business School (CIBS), Garki, Abuja; its purported Federal Capital Territory learning centre; and the University of America College of Science and Technology, also known as UAPOLY, Ekpoma, Edo State. Okonjo said the commission’s investigations showed that the institution was not accredited by any agency recognised by the United States Department of Education or the Council for Higher Education Accreditation (CHEA). She explained that its purported listing in the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), as well as claimed registrations in California and Florida, did not constitute accreditation or authorisation to award recognised university degrees. The NUC spokesperson also dismissed claims that the institution had obtained approval from the Federal Ministry of Education, the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board, the National Board for Technical Education and the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria. According to her, even if such approvals had been obtained, they would not confer the authority to operate a university or award degrees in Nigeria. The commission expressed concern over advertisements by the institution offering programmes in law, nursing science, engineering, pharmaceutical science, aerospace and rocket engineering, as well as postgraduate qualifications, including PhD degrees. It also raised concerns about promises of National Youth Service Corps mobilisation, professional recognition and opportunities to obtain green cards to live and work in the United States or Europe. Okonjo warned that qualifications obtained from unapproved institutions would not be recognised for NYSC mobilisation, professional registration with relevant Nigerian regulatory bodies or admission into the Nigerian Law School. She further cautioned that using reputable public institutions as venues for ceremonies did not amount to an endorsement or confer legitimacy on an unapproved university. The commission advised prospective students, parents and guardians against seeking admission, paying fees or participating in academic programmes organised by the institution and its affiliated centres, warning that individuals and organisations involved in the operations risked regulatory and legal action. University’s response Reacting to the development, the University of America, Curaçao, in a statement issued by its Media Consultant, Martins Chiedozie Ugwu, said it was established under the laws of Curaçao, a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It maintained that its authority to award degrees derived from its home jurisdiction and that it had never presented itself as a Nigerian university or claimed that its existence depended on a licence from the NUC. The institution said it possessed a government-issued operating licence, a ministerial charter authorising it to award academic degrees and institutional accreditation under Curaçao’s regulatory framework. It, however, acknowledged that recruiting students, establishing physical learning facilities and conducting educational activities in Nigeria were subject to applicable Nigerian laws and regulations. Addressing the facilities mentioned in the NUC notice, the university said CIBS, the purported FCT learning centre and UAPOLY were learning support centres rather than independent degree-awarding institutions. It explained that the centres were designed to provide students with internet access, tutorials, learning resources, library services and supervised examination support, where applicable, while enrolment and the award of qualifications remained the responsibility of the foreign institution. The university also argued that institutional licensing, government charters, accreditation, professional recognition and registration in international educational databases were distinct regulatory concepts. It said inclusion in an international database or registration in a foreign jurisdiction did not automatically amount to accreditation in Nigeria, just as the absence of Nigerian accreditation did not, in its view, invalidate the legal existence of a foreign institution in its home country. On concerns over NYSC mobilisation, professional registration and admission into the Nigerian Law School, the university acknowledged that recognition by Nigerian regulatory and professional bodies was separate from the validity of its foreign charter. It also referred to what it described as previous engagements and instances of graduate recognition relating to NYSC mobilisation, saying the claims could be verified through official correspondence and relevant records. The institution called on the NUC and the Federal Ministry of Education to engage it in a formal process to examine its operating licence, charter, accreditation documents, academic arrangements and the status of its learning support centres in Nigeria. It said it was willing to make relevant institutional documents available to the authorities and address legitimate regulatory concerns through lawful channels. The university urged the media to distinguish between allegations, regulatory findings and established legal facts in reporting the controversy, noting that the disagreement could affect students, graduates, parents and its institutional reputation. It maintained that disagreements over the regulation of educational activities in Nigeria should be treated separately from questions concerning the legal existence of a foreign institution in its home jurisdiction. The institution said its priority remained protecting the interests of its students and pursuing constructive engagement with Nigerian authorities. The post University of America challenges NUC over illegal operations appeared first on Vanguard News .

UG SRC rejects 15% hall fee increment, demands further reduction
items.description: The University of Ghana Students’ Representative Council (UGSRC) is demanding a further reduction in the proposed 15 per cent increase in hall fees, insisting the adjustment remains too expensive for the average student. The SRC says it does not accept the revised increment, despite negotiations with the University of Ghana Enterprise Limited (UGEL) reducing the initial proposal of 26 per cent. In a press briefing statement issued on November 19, 2026, the SRC disclosed that it met UGEL, Junior Common Room (JCR) executives and the Graduate Students’ Association of Ghana (GRASAG) on September 30, 2026, to discuss the proposed increase. According to the Council, UGEL initially proposed a 26 per cent increment, which was subsequently reduced to 15 per cent following what it described as intense negotiations.\ However, the SRC stressed that the revised figure was still unacceptable, arguing that it does not reflect the financial difficulties facing students and their parents. It is therefore calling on University Management and UGEL to review the proposed increment downwards to ensure that hall fees remain affordable. Beyond the proposed hall fee increase, the SRC is also demanding stronger regulation of private hostel charges around the Legon campus. It wants the University to establish a framework that sets an approved threshold for rent increases, a clearly defined academic-year calendar for adjustments and an enforceable Rent Control mechanism to prevent arbitrary increases by private hostel operators. The Council also wants the University to encourage more private investment in student accommodation to increase supply and ease pressure on existing facilities. It disclosed that University Management, in collaboration with the SRC, had established a structure to attract private investors and individuals interested in financing the construction of affordable student hostels. The SRC says its own hostel project forms part of the long-term effort to address the accommodation deficit. It has called on University Management, UGEL, private hostel operators and the government to work towards a sustainable solution, warning that rising accommodation costs are affecting students’ academic work and well-being.

items.title: Finding Love in Accra Episode 6: The morning after nothing happened
items.description: Read Also: Finding Love in Accra Episode 5: Dinner and other miscalculations “Start from the beginning,” Emefa said. “I cooked. He came. We ate. He has a girlfriend.” “That is a police statement. Give me the details.” I lay on my bed, still wearing the dress. By the time I finished, she had gone quiet. Then she asked, “But why didn’t you ask him directly?” “I asked about the woman.” “And when he didn’t answer?” “I got distracted.” “By what?” I looked at the ceiling. “His voice.” “Lovia.” “And his shoulders.” She sighed. “Did he know you thought it was a date?” “Emefa, there were candles.” “During these electricity tariffs, that could mean anything.” I laughed despite myself. Then, quite unexpectedly, I started crying. Not dramatic crying. Just a few tears that slipped into my ears while I lay there feeling stupid. “I really thought he wanted me.” Her voice softened. “I know.” “The way he spoke to me. The calls. He remembered everything.” “And you filled in what he didn’t say.” I wiped my face. I wanted to argue. Instead, I asked her to stay on the phone while I took off my makeup. Sunday morning, Kojo texted. I hope you slept well. I stared at it from under my duvet. What a bold hope. Another message followed. I’m sorry about last night. Can we talk? I wanted to reply immediately. That annoyed me more than the message. Even now, part of me wanted to hear his voice and let him explain everything into something less painful. I got up and went to the kitchen. Two wineglasses beside the sink. His plate stacked neatly beneath mine. Half a bottle of wine I had selected after consulting a shop attendant as though I were negotiating an international agreement. I put the glasses away. Then I answered. What exactly are we doing, Kojo? He called. I watched the phone ring before picking up. “Good morning.” “Morning.” “How are you?” “Embarrassed. You?” He exhaled. “Lovia, I never meant to hurt you.” “But you knew.” A pause. “You said you knew why I was asking about her.” “Yes.” “So when were you going to tell me?” “I should have told you then.” I sat at the kitchen table. “Are you happy with her?” The question escaped before I could stop it. There it was. One last little application for a vacancy that did not exist. “Yes,” he said quietly. “I am.” I pressed my lips together. “Okay.” “I missed you too, you know.” My eyes closed. “Please don’t.” “It’s true.” “Then miss me in a way that doesn’t confuse me.” He said nothing. I looked down at a tiny patch of candle wax on the table. “I can’t do the late-night calls. Or spend every morning waiting for your message while you have someone.” “I understand.” I hated how sensible he sounded. A small, unreasonable part of me had wanted a protest. “Take care, Kojo.” “You too, Lovia.” This time, I ended the call. By afternoon, I had muted his status. Not blocked. Let us not award me strength I had not yet developed. I also changed his contact name back to Kojo Campus . Whatever had happened after graduation was no longer my department. Emefa arrived carrying takeaway and wearing the expression of someone determined not to say I told you so . We ate straight from the containers.

items.title: Fountain of Life denies closure amid leadership crisis
items.description: By OLAYINKA LATONA LAGOS — The Fountain of Life Church has denied reports that its premises have been sealed, insisting that the church remains open, although access to its facilities is currently restricted amid an ongoing leadership dispute. The church, in a post on its official Instagram page, shared a graphic bearing the inscription, “DON’T BELIEVE THE NOISE! CHURCH IS NOT SEALED,” while inviting worshippers to attend its Sunday service. The clarification comes amid a leadership crisis involving Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and the church’s board, which has generated public attention in recent days. However, a visit by Vanguard correspondents to the church premises revealed restricted access, with activities appearing limited. There was no visible presence of police personnel at the premises, while private security operatives were stationed at the entrance. Efforts by a Vanguard reporter to gain access to the church were unsuccessful, as a security official said only persons with official business within the premises would be allowed in. The restricted access comes despite the church’s public invitation to worshippers to attend Sunday’s service. The church had earlier announced the postponement of its 2026 Thanksgiving Service, initially scheduled for Sunday, November 22, stating that a new date would be communicated. The developments come against the backdrop of a legal battle over the church’s leadership. The Lagos State High Court had restrained Odukoya from holding himself out as Senior Pastor and Spiritual Head of the church following an application by the church’s Incorporated Trustees. Justice O.O. Adewunmi-Oshin granted the interim orders on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, in a suit filed by the trustees. The court also restrained Odukoya, whether acting personally or through proxies, from interfering with, disrupting or obstructing the church’s activities, governance and other operations. The orders were granted ex parte, meaning they were made without first hearing Odukoya’s response to the application. However, the court preserved his right to apply to set aside the orders or respond to the substantive claims after being served with the court processes. The case was adjourned until December 1, 2026, for mention. The leadership dispute became public on November 17, when a faction of the church’s Board of Trustees announced that it no longer recognised Odukoya as senior pastor, citing a succession video reportedly recorded by the late founder, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, in December 2021. The trustees subsequently named Pastor Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader. However, Odukoya and the church leadership rejected the decision, maintaining that his appointment as senior pastor in September 2023 was valid. items.title: IA: importante baisse des offres d'emploi dans les métiers les plus exposés
items.description: L'avènement de l'intelligence artificielle générative depuis quatre ans a provoqué une diminution des offres d’emplois dans les métiers les plus exposés, selon une étude de Coface. Pour un métier avec une exposition à l'IA de 10%, c'est-à-dire dont le contenu est à 10% automatisable, le nombre d'annonces de recrutement à France Travail a diminué de 12,4 % au troisième trimestre, ont constaté les économistes Axelle Arquié et Aurélien Duthoit, auteurs de l'étude. Avec la même méthodologie, ils sont parvenus à des résultats similaires auprès des services publics de l’emploi en Allemagne, avec 10,2 % d'annonces en moins, et en Suède (-10,8 %), malgré des structures économiques très différentes dans ces pays. Ce sont ainsi 25.000 annonces en moins qui sont parues chez France Travail sur le trimestre en raison de l'IA, d'après l'étude. Les métiers les plus impactés sont souvent transverses, présents dans un grand nombre de secteurs. Ainsi les ressources humaines, qui comptent 25,9 % de tâches dès aujourd'hui automatisables, ont vu le nombre d'offres d’emploi décrocher de 42,8 % par rapport à la moyenne des secteurs où les postes de RH sont implantés. Les forces de vente (dont le télémarketing), la comptabilité-gestion, les systèmes d'information et de télécommunications, la conception et la R&D dans l'industrie ou le bâtiment sont également fortement impactés. « Cette corrélation entre le fait qu'un métier soit exposé à l'IA et que ses annonces d’emploi se dégradent n'existait pas » dans les études précédentes, a expliqué à l'AFP Aurélien Duthoit. Et contrairement à une idée reçue, la réduction des offres d’emploi ne concerne pas que les nouveaux entrants sur le marché du travail : pour les postes exigeant moins d'un an d'expérience, elle est de 14 %, contre 19,4 % entre un et deux ans, 14,1 % entre deux et quatre ans de 16 % au-delà de quatre ans. L'IA ne provoque pas encore une vague de licenciements en Europe parce que « les entreprises attendent, elles ne sont pas bien sûres de comment adopter la technologie », selon Axelle Arquié. Mais « quand la récession frappe et qu'elles sont obligées de faire des économies, elles automatisent massivement », prévient-elle. Aux Etats-Unis, la croissance de l’emploi chez les cols blancs a déjà décroché depuis le lancement de l'IA générative pour le grand public fin 2022, alors même que la hausse de la valeur ajoutée de ces emplois s'est accélérée, selon des données compilées par les auteurs. De son côté, l'Observatoire de France Travail souligne mardi dans une autre étude que les métiers d'aide comptable, assistant juridique ou secrétaire administrative comptent parmi ceux où le risque de « substitution de l’humain » par l'IA est le plus fort. Les offres d’emploi dans le secrétariat ont baissé depuis 2022 d'environ 40 %, sans toutefois que l'organisme puisse établir formellement le lien avec le développement de l'IA.
